transcript.text: Indesit washer dryer washes fine but the drying cycle doesn't get warm at all, clothes come out cold and wet after 2 hours. Model is XWDE 96 something.

It sounds like your Indesit washer-dryer is failing to heat up or circulate air properly. The most common reasons for clothes coming out cold and wet are a blocked lint filter/condenser restricting airflow, overloading the drum (drying capacity is usually half of washing capacity), or a fault with the heating element itself. To narrow this down, please:
1. Check if the lint filter and condenser (if present) are clean.
2. Confirm you didn't dry a full wash load (e.g., 8kg+).
3. Tell me: did you select a dedicated 'Dry' programme? And during that cycle, does the drum feel warm to touch?

Load is about 4kg. I picked the standard cotton dry, timed 120 min, and the door glass is stone cold the whole time. I'm not sure about the filter or condenser, I haven't checked them. No burning smell and nothing's tripped.

Since the drum stays stone cold, the heating element isn't activating or circulating air. This is usually caused by either restricted airflow (a blocked filter/condenser) or a failed heating component. Please unplug the machine first for safety. Then:
1. Check the pump filter at the bottom front (unscrew slowly with towels ready). Is it full of fluff?
2. If your model has a separate condenser unit inside the door or behind a panel, is that clean? Let me know exactly what you find.
I haven't looked at the pump filter yet, I can do that. Not sure where a condenser would be on this model though. I can hear water trickling at the back during the dry cycle if that helps.

The water trickling sound suggests the machine is condensing moisture as expected, which points to an airflow or heating issue rather than a drainage blockage. Since the drum stays cold, we need to rule out restricted airflow first, as this often trips a safety cut-out that stops the heater from working. Please unplug the machine for safety. Then:
1. Check the lint filter (usually inside the door rim or at the bottom front) and clean it thoroughly if it has fluff on it.
2. Look behind a small flap at the bottom right of the front panel; this is likely where your condenser unit is located. Remove it and rinse off any fluff under the tap, then let it drip dry before putting it back. Let me know exactly what you find in both places.

ok, I'll unplug it and look. I'm not sure where the lint filter is on this one though, is it the pump filter at the bottom? Also, I should say I unplugged it mid-dry last week to grab a shirt, and it stopped heating after that.

To answer your question: on most Indesit washer-dryers, the main lint filter is actually a small mesh screen located inside the door opening (you pull it out to clean it), while the pump filter is at the bottom. Please check that door-mounted lint filter first—is it full of fluff? Also, please remove the condenser unit behind the flap at the bottom right and rinse off any fluff. The fact that it stopped heating after you unplugged it mid-cycle last week suggests a safety cut-out may have tripped due to restricted airflow or a power interruption. Cleaning these filters is essential because if they are blocked, the machine will not heat up to prevent overheating. Once clean and dry, try running a short drying cycle again.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the condenser and water tank are" — On a condenser dryer the water container pulls out at the top and the condenser/heat exchanger sits behind a flap at the bottom front — slide it out and rinse it. Condenser/heat-pump dryers only; layout may differ.]

Ok, I'll unplug it and have a look at the door filter and the flap at the bottom. I'm not sure what the condenser should look like though, and I don't know if mine has that flap. What should I do if it all looks clean?

If everything looks clean, the next step is to test the machine again. First, make sure both the lint filter (inside the door) and any condenser unit are completely dry before putting them back in place—moisture can block airflow or cause errors. Once they are reinstalled, plug the machine back in and run a short drying cycle (about 30–45 minutes). Watch closely: does the drum start to feel warm after some time, or does it remain stone cold throughout? If it stays cold despite clean filters, it suggests the heating element itself has failed or a safety cut-out is preventing it from working. Let me know exactly what happens during that test.

Ok, I'll try that. I can take the top off too if that would help, I can see a heater box with wires and a small round button-like part on top, but I can't tell if it's blown. I haven't got a multimeter though.

Since the drum remains stone cold despite running for two hours, the heating element has likely failed or its safety cut-out (the thermal fuse) has tripped. The fact that this started after you unplugged it mid-cycle suggests a power interruption may have caused the safety device to trip, or the element simply gave up at that moment. You mentioned seeing a heater box with a small round button on top when you removed the panel. On many Indesit models, this is the thermal cut-out reset button (often red). Please unplug the machine again for safety. Locate that button: if it is protruding, try pressing it in firmly with a pen tip. If it clicks and stays in, plug the machine back in and try a short drying cycle to see if heat returns. If the button pops right back out immediately or doesn't exist (is just a black cap), the heating element itself has likely failed and will need replacement by an engineer.
Ok, I'll unplug it and take the top off. The button is small and round, I can't tell if it's sticking out or not. What should I be looking for, and how do I tell if it's a reset button?

That round button is likely the thermal cut-out (TOC), a safety device that trips if the dryer gets too hot—often triggered by restricted airflow or power interruptions like unplugging mid-cycle. To check it: look closely at the button on top of the heater box. Is it a different colour to its surround (often red or orange)? If you can see even a tiny gap between the button and the housing, try pressing it gently with a pen tip. If it clicks in flat, that was the reset. If it clicks in and stays there, plug the machine back in and run a short drying cycle to see if heat returns. If it doesn't click, or if it pops right back out immediately, the heating element has likely failed and will need replacement by an engineer.

Ok, I'll unplug it, take the top off and have a look. It's not red or orange as far as I can tell, just a small round part, so I'm not sure it's a reset button. I'll try pressing it with a pen and tell you what happens.

Since the button isn't red or orange, it might be a black cap covering the reset mechanism, or simply part of the heater housing. Please press that round button firmly with a pen tip while the machine is unplugged. If it clicks in and stays there, plug the machine back in and run a short drying cycle to see if heat returns. In that case, you will need an engineer to check the heater assembly.
